Three-point quadratic reproduction forces the identity filter ((w−1​,w0​,w1​)=(0,1,0))

Words: 60
Time series OurBigBook.com
A symmetric three-point smoother with weights (a,b,a) reproduces constants only if 2a+b=1. Reproducing quadratic trends also requires 2a=0, so a=0 and b=1. Thus the identity estimator Xt​ is unbiased, but there is no nontrivial three-point linear smoother reproducing every quadratic. An assertion excluding even the identity estimator is false. This clarifies why the five-point symmetric quadratic trend smoother is the first symmetric nontrivial example.

Five-point symmetric quadratic trend smoother ((−3,12,17,12,−3)/35)

Words: 84
Time series OurBigBook.com
For observations Xt​=Tt​+εt​ with a quadratic trend and uncorrelated equal-variance errors, a symmetric five-point linear filter of a stationary time series has weights (a,b,c,b,a). Reproducing every quadratic requires 2a+2b+c=1 and 8a+2b=0. Substitution gives b=−4a, c=1+6a and error variance σ2(70a2+12a+1). Its unique minimum occurs at a=−3/35, producing the displayed weights and variance 17σ2/35. Negative weights are allowed: this is a linear weighted smoother, not a convex average. Applying a linear filter to a deterministic trend plus stationary errors does not assert that the complete observation process is stationary.

Turning point test of randomness (E[PT​]=2(T−2)/3,Var(PT​)=(16T−29)/90)

Words: 85
Time series OurBigBook.com
For independent identically distributed continuous observations, count strict local maxima and minima at interior positions. Each turning indicator has probability 2/3, adjacent indicators have joint probability 5/12, indicators two positions apart have joint probability 9/20, and more distant indicators are independent. Summing these covariances gives the displayed variance for T≥4. The indicators form a bounded 2-dependent sequence, giving an asymptotically normal standardized count. Too few turns suggests persistent trends; too many suggests alternation. Ties and dependent observations require a different calibration.

Exponential smoothing (St​=KXt​+(1−K)St−1​)

Words: 266 Articles: 4
Time series OurBigBook.com
With a fixed gain 0<K<1, exponential smoothing recursively combines the newest observation with the preceding estimate. Iteration assigns geometric weights K(1−K)j to older observations, together with a diminishing weight on the initial estimate. The steady-state local-level Kalman gain gives a probabilistic interpretation of this recursion.

Double exponential smoothing

Words: 168 Articles: 2
Exponential smoothing OurBigBook.com
Double exponential smoothing supplements a smoothed level with a smoothed slope so that forecasts can extrapolate a local linear trend. Two common versions are Holt's linear trend method, with separate level and slope gains, and Brown's double exponential smoothing, which applies the same smoothing gain twice. They are different algorithms, not two names for one recursion. Neither version by itself models seasonal variation.

Brown's double exponential smoothing (at​=2st(1)​−st(2)​,bt​=1−αα​(st(1)​−st(2)​))

Words: 58
Double exponential smoothing OurBigBook.com
For 0<α<1, set st(1)​=αXt​+(1−α)st−1(1)​ and st(2)​=αst(1)​+(1−α)st−1(2)​. Use the displayed corrected level and slope, then forecast at​+hbt​. For an exact linear trend after initialization transients, the first and second smooths have lags (1−α)/α and twice that lag; their difference recovers the slope and the corrected level removes the lag. This is distinct from Holt's linear trend method.

Holt's linear trend method (Xt+h∣t​=ℓt​+hbt​)

Words: 53
Double exponential smoothing OurBigBook.com
Update the level and slope by ℓt​=αXt​+(1−α)(ℓt−1​+bt−1​) and bt​=β(ℓt​−ℓt−1​)+(1−β)bt−1​, with gains in (0,1). The first update compares the new observation with the previous level extrapolated one step; the second smooths the latest level increment. The displayed forecast extrapolates that local slope. This is a double exponential smoothing method for a nonseasonal trending time series.

Simple exponential smoothing (ℓt​=αXt​+(1−α)ℓt−1​)

Words: 56
Exponential smoothing OurBigBook.com
For 0<α<1, update a local level by the displayed recursion and forecast every future horizon by ℓt​. Iteration gives geometrically decreasing weights α(1−α)j on past observations and a vanishing contribution from the initial level. It is useful for a locally stable level without a persistent trend or seasonality. A trend causes lag, motivating double exponential smoothing.

Wold decomposition (Xt​=Dt​+∑j≥0​cj​ϵt−j​)

Words: 52
Time series OurBigBook.com
A second-order stationary time series decomposes into a deterministic component and a one-sided square-summable linear filter of a stationary time series of its mutually orthogonal linear innovations. Normalize c0​=1. For a causal invertible ARMA process with no deterministic component, the driving white noise is this innovation process: observations and innovations span the same closed past subspace, while the next innovation is orthogonal to it.

Best linear prediction from a finite past (Xt∣T​=projspan(X1​,…,XT​)​Xt​)

Words: 365 Articles: 6
Time series OurBigBook.com
The best mean-square linear predictor is orthogonal projection onto the span of the available centered observations, plus the known mean. Orthogonal innovations give a convenient basis of that span. Prediction at a future horizon must use only actually observed variables; it need not be a one-step predictor.

Recursive forecasts of an autoregressive process (XT,k​=m+∑j=1p​ϕj​(XT,k−j​−m))

Words: 135 Articles: 1
Best linear prediction from a finite past OurBigBook.com
For a causal autoregressive process with mean m and innovations orthogonal to the observed past, define XT,h​=XT+h​ for h≤0 and replace future innovations by zero. The displayed recursion is its best linear prediction from a finite past when at least the last p observations are available. Future innovation sums are orthogonal to those observations, which proves the projection property. Mere white noise does not guarantee that a linear forecast equals a conditional mean: that stronger interpretation requires martingale-difference or independent innovations.

Forecasts of an integrated AR(1) process (WT,k​=WT​+kμ+1−ϕϕ(1−ϕk)​(WT​−WT−1​−μ))

Words: 64
Recursive forecasts of an autoregressive process OurBigBook.com
If the increments of W have mean μ and centered increments satisfy a causal autoregressive process of order one with ∣ϕ∣<1, sum their recursive forecasts to obtain the displayed expression. For fixed forecast origin, WT,k​/k→μ. One must observe the last increment, requiring T≥2 or a known initial level W0​; a single observed level without an initial-level model does not identify that increment.

Finite-past innovation (Ut​=Xt​−projspan(X1​,…,Xt−1​)​Xt​)

Words: 53
Best linear prediction from a finite past OurBigBook.com
Starting observations at a finite time, subtract the best linear predictor based on the available earlier observations. The resulting residual is orthogonal to their linear span. The unit-triangular relation between observations and residuals makes the residuals an orthogonal basis of the same finite observation space. These differ from infinite-past innovations until the initialization effect disappears.

Two-step prediction for an MA(1) process (XT+2∣T​=0)

Words: 40
Best linear prediction from a finite past OurBigBook.com
In a centered MA(1) process, XT+2​ is uncorrelated with every observation through time T. Its best linear predictor from that information is therefore zero, with error variance σ2(1+θ2). One-step innovation formulas using XT+1​ cannot be substituted when that observation is unavailable.

Finite-sample innovations of an MA(1) process (λt​=γ1​/φt−1​,φt​=γ0​−γ1​λt​)

Words: 94 Articles: 1
Best linear prediction from a finite past OurBigBook.com
Starting at time one, the orthogonal residuals satisfy Ut​=Xt​−λt​Ut−1​, with λt​=γ1​/φt−1​ and φt​=γ0​−γ1​λt​. Earlier innovation directions have zero covariance with the new observation. Explicitly, with Sm​=∑j=0m​θ2j, φt​=σ2St​/St−1​ and λt​=θSt−2​/St−1​ for t≥2. These formulas follow by induction from St​=(1+θ2)St−1​−θ2St−2​, with S0​=1 and S1​=1+θ2. This includes θ=±1, where φt​=σ2(t+1)/t.

Limiting MA(1) innovations coefficient (λ∞​=θ (∣θ∣≤1),λ∞​=1/θ (∣θ∣>1))

Words: 39
Finite-sample innovations of an MA(1) process OurBigBook.com
For an MA(1) process, the recursion λt​=θ/(1+θ2−θλt−1​) has candidate limits θ and 1/θ. The limit in [−1,1] is θ when ∣θ∣≤1 and 1/θ otherwise. The limiting innovation variance is σ2max(1,θ2), expressing the same covariance law through an invertible reciprocal representation.

Best linear prediction from an infinite past (Xt+1​=projHt​​Xt+1​)

Words: 50
Time series OurBigBook.com
The best mean-square linear predictor from a semi-infinite past is the orthogonal projection onto the closed linear span of past observations in the random-variable Hilbert space. For a causal invertible ARMA representation, past observations and past innovations generate the same closed span. The next linear innovation is orthogonal to it and is therefore the prediction error.

State-space model (time series, St​=FSt−1​+Zt​,Yt​=HSt​+Wt​)

Words: 302 Articles: 5
Time series OurBigBook.com
A state-space model separates a latent transition equation St​=FSt−1​+Zt​ from an observation equation Yt​=HSt​+Wt​. A complete specification includes the initial-state law and its relation to the noise sequences, not just the two equations. Linear second-order models specify covariance structure; Gaussian versions additionally prescribe joint Gaussian laws.

Three-coordinate state realization of an ARMA(1,1) process OurBigBook.com
For ∣ϕ∣<1 and centered independent white noise values, the state above has expected value zero and this stationary covariance matrix, where γ0​=σ2(1+θ2+2ϕθ)/(1−ϕ2). Local-level state-space model (Xt​=St​+vt​,St​=St−1​+wt​)

Words: 61
State-space model (time series) OurBigBook.com
The latent state follows a random walk, while observations add independent measurement noise. If the two noises have variances W,V, the differences have autocovariances W+2V at lag zero, −V at lag one, and zero at larger lags. For V,W>0, write q=(W+2V+W2+4WV​)/2 and ϑ=−V/q. The differenced process is an invertible moving-average model with coefficient ϑ and innovation variance q. Its level has a unit root.

Gaussian innovation likelihood (ℓ=−21​∑t​[logdetΣt​+ϵt⊤​Σt−1​ϵt​+qlog(2π)])

Words: 66
State-space model (time series) OurBigBook.com
In a linear Gaussian state-space model, let the predicted state mean and covariance be mt−​,Pt−​. The observation innovation process has conditional mean zero and covariance Σt​=APt−​A⊤+R, with innovation ϵt​=yt​−Amt−​. The conditional multivariate normal distribution gives the predictive observation density. Multiplying these conditional densities by the chain rule gives the displayed likelihood function; equivalently the innovations are independent Gaussian vectors. The Kalman filter supplies mt−​,Pt−​ recursively, so one evaluates the exact observed-data likelihood function without integrating all latent states jointly.

Stationary initialization of a scalar linear state-space model (S0​=∑j≥0​ϕjZ−j​)

Words: 54
State-space model (time series) OurBigBook.com
For ∣ϕ∣<1, initialize the state by S0​=∑j≥0​ϕjZ−j​, with variance σz2​/(1−ϕ2). It is orthogonal to future state noise and to observation noise orthogonal to all state noise. Under a Gaussian specification, take the initial state Gaussian with this variance and independent of future noises. Starting at zero instead gives a transient model.

Anticausal time series (Xt​=−∑j≥1​ϕ−jZt+j​)

Words: 34
Time series OurBigBook.com
An anticausal noise representation uses future rather than present and past innovations. For a two-sided AR(1) equation with ∣ϕ∣>1, the stationary solution is Xt​=−∑j≥1​ϕ−jZt+j​. Thus stationary existence alone does not require causality.

Linear process (time series, Xt​=μ+∑j​ψj​εt−j​)

Words: 83 Articles: 1
Time series OurBigBook.com
A linear process is an L2-convergent white-noise filter Xt​=μ+∑j∈Z​ψj​εt−j​, with square-summable coefficients. It is weakly stationary, and its autocovariance is σε2​∑j​ψj​ψj+h​. A causal representation restricts the coefficients to j≥0; it is then an infinite moving-average representation.

Two-geometric-coefficient expansion of a causal ARMA(2,1) process (ψj​=arj+dsj)

Words: 45
Linear process (time series) OurBigBook.com
When the transfer function is (1+θz)/((1−rz)(1−sz)) with distinct r,s of modulus less than one, partial fractions give coefficients ψj​=arj+dsj, where a+d=1 and −as−dr=θ. White-noise orthogonality gives covariance at lag h≥0 as σ2[a2rh/(1−r2)+d2sh/(1−s2)+ad(rh+sh)/(1−rs)]. This combines stable recursion with a closed geometric-sum covariance.

Autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity (σt2​=α0​+∑j​αj​Xt−j2​)

Words: 181 Articles: 4
Time series OurBigBook.com
An ARCH model writes Xt​=σt​εt​ with standardized independent driving noise and a conditional variance σt2​=α0​+∑j=1p​αj​Xt−j2​. Typically α0​>0 and αj​≥0 ensure a positive conditional variance. It allows a changing conditional scale even when X is a stationary process.

Sign symmetry of an ARCH process

Words: 43
Autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity OurBigBook.com
With symmetric driving noise whose sign is independent of its magnitude, changing the sign of one driving variable changes the corresponding Xt​ but leaves future conditional scales unchanged. Consequently Cov(Xt​,f(Xt+h​))=0 for h>0 and square-integrable f(Xt+h​). This conclusion uses symmetry, beyond the martingale difference sequence property.

Lag-two ARCH process (Xt​=α0​+α2​Xt−22​​εt​)

Words: 67 Articles: 1
Autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity OurBigBook.com
For α0​>0 and 0<α2​<1, the model Xt​=α0​+α2​Xt−22​​εt​ splits into independent even-time and odd-time chains in its stationary causal solution. With standard normal noise, EXt2​=α0​/(1−α2​), and its fourth moment is finite exactly when 3α22​<1.

Parity decomposition of a lag-two ARCH process

Words: 32
Lag-two ARCH process OurBigBook.com
The stationary squared process has the positive series Xt2​=α0​∑k≥0​α2k​∏j=0k​εt−2j2​. Even and odd observations therefore use disjoint families of independent random variables. This explains zero lag-one covariance of the squares despite dependence at lag two.

Volatility clustering

Words: 36
Autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity OurBigBook.com
Volatility clustering means that large absolute observations tend to be followed by further large absolute observations, and small ones by small ones. In an ARCH process, persistence is in the conditional variance rather than necessarily in the signed observations.

Seasonality

Words: 140 Articles: 1
Time series OurBigBook.com
Seasonality is systematic repetition at a calendar period. It can appear in a deterministic mean, in a periodic variance, or in dependence across seasons. A seasonal difference operator removes a fixed periodic mean but seasonal differencing does not remove periodic variance. A periodic-looking path alone does not prove a nonstationary process.

Seasonal extraction by a centred moving average

Words: 99
Seasonality OurBigBook.com
For an additive time series Xt​=Tt​+St​+εt​ with period-m seasonal component and ∑j=1m​Sj​=0, a centred average spanning one complete period removes the seasonal component while estimating the slowly varying trend. When m is even, average two adjacent length-m averages to centre the filter on an observation; the endpoints receive half the usual weights. Estimate each seasonal phase by averaging the corresponding detrended residuals across cycles, then subtract the mean of those phase averages to enforce the zero-sum convention. Multiplicative seasonality instead uses ratios and a mean-one convention. Repeated averaging is filter composition and induces serial dependence even from white noise.

Long-memory time series

Words: 41
Time series OurBigBook.com
A weakly stationary process can have very slowly decaying autocovariance, for example γ(h)∼Ch−β with C>0 and 0<β<1. Its sample mean can require a normalization different from T​. Long memory is dependence over long lags, rather than a changing marginal distribution.

Short-memory time series (∑h​∣γ(h)∣<∞)

Words: 31
Time series OurBigBook.com
In a second-order sense a weakly stationary process has short memory when its autocovariance is absolutely summable. Then its spectral density of a stationary process is continuous and its sample-mean variance has the usual finite long-run variance of a stationary process. A central limit theorem still needs additional conditions.

Periodically correlated process (γt+S​(h)=γt​(h))

Words: 37
Time series OurBigBook.com
A process has period-S second-order statistics when EXt+S​=EXt​ and Cov(Xt+S​,Xs+S​)=Cov(Xt​,Xs​) for all times. Its variance can vary by season, so it need not be a weakly stationary process. A periodic covariance period need not be the fundamental period.

Differencing (Δ=1−B)

Words: 101 Articles: 2
Time series OurBigBook.com
The difference ΔXt​=Xt​−Xt−1​ can remove a unit-root stochastic trend. A seasonal difference operator instead subtracts an observation a full seasonal period earlier. Neither operation automatically removes a changing variance.

Seasonal difference operator (ΔS​=1−BS)

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Differencing OurBigBook.com
For an integer period S, ΔS​Xt​=Xt​−Xt−S​ uses the backshift operator as 1−BS. It annihilates a deterministic period-S mean. If Xt​=mt​+εt​ with mt+S​=mt​ and strong white noise, the result is the stationary moving average εt​−εt−S​.

Seasonal differencing does not remove periodic variance

Words: 40
Seasonal difference operator OurBigBook.com
If Xt​=ct​εt​ with a deterministic periodic scale ct​=ct−S​ and strong white noise of variance σ2, then ΔS​Xt​=ct​(εt​−εt−S​). Its variance is 2σ2ct2​, still seasonal when ct2​ varies. A periodic scale model or variance standardization is more appropriate than blindly applying differencing.

Normalize the autoregressive and moving-average polynomials to have constant coefficient one, cancel common factors, and require all their zeros to lie outside the closed unit disk. With positive innovation variance these conditions give a causal, invertible, minimal Gaussian process representation. To prove identifiability, compare two such models with the same time-series spectral density. The ratio of their scaled rational transfer functions and its reciprocal are analytic on a neighbourhood of the closed unit disk and have modulus one on its boundary. The maximum modulus principle makes the ratio constant; its positive value at zero forces equality of the innovation variances and equality of the rational functions. Coprimality and the constant-coefficient normalization then force equality of both polynomials. Without the root restrictions, reciprocal root reflection of an ARMA representation and a rescaling of the innovation variance can preserve the spectrum, so the unrestricted parameters are not identifiable.

Applying that inverse also proves uniqueness among bounded second-moment solutions. A root on the unit circle forces the candidate spectral density of a stationary process to have a nonintegrable singularity. The stronger causality root criterion for an autoregressive model requires every root outside the closed unit disk.
